passages.happening:
Abraham is old now, “and the LORD had blessed him in every way” (verse 1). He calls the chief servant of his household and makes him swear an oath: “Place your hand under my thigh” (verse 2).

The servant must not take a wife for Isaac “from the daughters of the Canaanites” (verse 3). He must go to Abraham's own country and family to find one (verse 4).

The servant asks, “What if the woman is unwilling to follow me to this land? Shall I then take your son back to the land from which you came?” (verse 5). Abraham answers, “Make sure that you do not take my son back there” (verse 6). God “will send His angel before you” (verse 7). If the woman will not come, the servant is free of the oath (verse 8).

The servant swears (verse 9).
passages.hearers:
The servant is never named in the whole chapter. He is simply Abraham's servant, ‘who managed all he owned’. Some readers think he is Eliezer of Damascus, named in 15:2, but the text does not say.

The hand ‘under my thigh’ was a solemn way to swear. It is usually understood to touch the place of a man's offspring, tying the oath to Abraham's descendants. Jacob asks for the same oath before he dies (47:29).

Why not a Canaanite wife? Abraham's worry is not only family pride. His heir must not be pulled into the worship of the gods of the land. Later, Esau's Canaanite wives bring grief to Isaac and Rebekah (26:34-35).

And why must Isaac not go back? Because the land is God's promise. Abraham left Haran at God's word. His son must not undo that. The bride will come to the land; the son will not leave it.

Notice Abraham's faith. He does not know who the woman is. He does know that God will go ahead of the servant. He also leaves room for the woman to say no.
passages.later:
Israel's law later warns against marriages that would turn God's people to other gods: “they will turn your sons away from following Me to serve other gods” (Deuteronomy 7:4). Paul gives Christians a similar warning: “Do not be unequally yoked with unbelievers” (2 Corinthians 6:14).

Jacob asks Joseph for the same kind of oath: “put your hand under my thigh and promise to show me kindness and faithfulness” (Genesis 47:29).
passages.asks: Abraham trusted God to go ahead of his servant, but he still gave him clear instructions and left the woman free to refuse. Ask how you hold faith and careful planning together. Then ask whether you leave other people free to say no.

passages.happening:
The servant takes ten of his master's camels and many gifts, and travels to Nahor's town in Aram-naharaim (verse 10). At evening he makes the camels kneel by the well, “at the time when the women went out to draw water” (verse 11).

“O LORD, God of my master Abraham,” he prayed, “please grant me success today, and show kindness to my master Abraham” (verse 12). He asks for a sign. Let the right girl be the one who says, “Drink, and I will water your camels as well” (verse 14).

“Before the servant had finished praying, Rebekah came out with her jar on her shoulder” (verse 15). He asks for a drink. “Drink, my lord,” she replied (verse 18). Then she says, “I will also draw water for your camels, until they have had enough to drink” (verse 19). She runs back and forth until all the camels have drunk (verse 20).

He gives her a gold ring and two gold bracelets, and asks whose daughter she is. She is the granddaughter of Abraham's brother Nahor (verses 22-24). The servant bows and worships: “the LORD has led me on the journey to the house of my master’s relatives” (verse 27).
passages.hearers:
Aram-naharaim means ‘Aram of the two rivers’, the land of upper Mesopotamia near Haran, hundreds of miles to the north-east. It was a long trip.

Wells were natural meeting places, and drawing water at evening was women's work. The servant goes where he would most likely meet the young women of the town.

Look closely at the sign he asks for. It is not a coin toss. A woman who would give a tired stranger water, and then offer, on her own, to water ten thirsty camels, is generous, strong and hardworking. A thirsty camel can drink a great deal, and every jar had to be carried up from the spring by hand. The sign tests character.

The camels raise a question. A 2013 study by Tel Aviv University found that domesticated camels in the Aravah valley, south of the Dead Sea, appear mostly from the last part of the 900s BC. Some take the camels in Genesis as written in the terms of a later age. Others reply that camels were rare but known earlier, and the debate goes on.

Rebekah does everything quickly. The word ‘quickly’ comes twice, and she ‘ran’. She is not a passive figure. She is the most active person in the scene.

The servant ‘watched her silently’ (verse 21). He does not jump to a conclusion. He waits to see. Then he asks about her family, and only then does he worship. God never speaks in this chapter, yet the servant sees his hand at work.
passages.later:
The scholar Robert Alter, in The Art of Biblical Narrative (1981), called repeated scenes like this ‘type-scenes’. A traveler meets a future bride at a well three times: here, Jacob and Rachel (Genesis 29:9-11), and Moses and Zipporah (Exodus 2:15-17).

John's Gospel sets Jesus at a well too: “Jesus, weary from His journey, sat down by the well” (John 4:6), and a Samaritan woman comes to draw water (John 4:7). Many readers hear this old pattern behind that meeting.

The wise prayer for guidance is still the servant's kind: “Commit your way to the LORD; trust in Him, and He will do it” (Psalm 37:5). “If any of you lacks wisdom, he should ask God” (James 1:5).
passages.hard:
Should Christians ask God for a sign, as the servant did? Readers answer in more than one way.

Some take the servant as a model: ask God to show you what to do in a specific way. Others are careful, because the Bible also says, “Do not test the LORD your God” (Deuteronomy 6:16).

The chapter suggests a middle path. The servant's sign was wise, not random: it tested a woman's kindness. He went where his master told him. He watched before he spoke. Genesis tells what happened this time; it does not give a method. Most Christian traditions teach that guidance usually comes through Scripture, prayer, wisdom and the counsel of others, while God can and sometimes does answer a specific request.

This chapter is not a method for finding a husband or wife. No one should wait at a well, or anywhere else, for a sign that picks a person for them. What the chapter does show is worth looking for: kindness to strangers, hard work, faith and family who pray.
passages.asks: The servant prayed, then watched, then worshiped. Ask whether you pray about your decisions and then look for God's answer with patience. Then ask whether, like Rebekah, you are the kind of person who does more than was asked.

passages.happening:
Rebekah runs home and tells her mother's household (verse 28). Her brother Laban sees the ring and the bracelets and runs out to the man: “Come, you who are blessed by the LORD” (verse 31). The camels are unloaded and fed, and water is brought to wash the men's feet (verse 32).

A meal is served, but the servant says, “I will not eat until I have told you what I came to say” (verse 33).

He tells the whole story. “I am Abraham’s servant,” he replied (verse 34). God has blessed his master. Sarah bore a son in her old age, and Abraham has given him everything (verses 35-36). He tells of the oath, the prayer at the spring, and Rebekah's answer (verses 37-48). Then he asks: “Now if you will show kindness and faithfulness to my master, tell me; but if not, let me know, so that I may go elsewhere” (verse 49).
passages.hearers:
Laban runs out after he sees the gold. Readers who know the rest of Genesis will notice that. Years later Laban will cheat Rebekah's son Jacob (chapters 29 to 31). Here, already, his eyes go to the jewelry.

The servant will not eat until his errand is told. He wants the matter settled before anything else.

His retelling is careful. He stresses Abraham's wealth and God's blessing. He leaves out Abraham's worry that Isaac might go back. He tells the order of events a little differently, so that he seems to have asked about her family before he gave her the gold. He is a wise speaker, and the storyteller trusts the reader to notice.

‘Kindness and faithfulness’ is a pair of words the Bible uses for loyal love: love that keeps its promises. The servant prayed that God would show it to Abraham (verse 12), and praised God for showing it (verse 27). Now he asks the family to show it too.
passages.later: The pair ‘kindness and faithfulness’ appears at Sinai, when God describes himself as “abounding in loving devotion and faithfulness” (Exodus 34:6). John says of Jesus that he was “full of grace and truth” (John 1:14).
passages.asks: The servant put his master's errand before his own dinner. Ask what task God has given you that you keep setting aside for comfort. Then notice how the servant told the truth with wisdom, choosing what to stress without saying anything false.

passages.happening:
Laban and Bethuel answer, “This is from the LORD; we have no choice in the matter” (verse 50). “Rebekah is here before you. Take her and go” (verse 51). The servant bows to the ground before the LORD (verse 52). He gives gifts of silver, gold and clothing to Rebekah, and precious gifts to her brother and mother (verse 53).

In the morning he wants to leave at once. Her brother and mother ask for ten days or so (verse 55). He says, “Do not delay me” (verse 56).

So they said, “We will call the girl and ask her opinion” (verse 57). They called Rebekah and asked her, “Will you go with this man?” “I will go,” she replied (verse 58).

They send her off with her nurse and bless her: “Our sister, may you become the mother of thousands upon thousands. May your offspring possess the gates of their enemies” (verse 60). Rebekah and her servant girls mount the camels and follow the man (verse 61).
passages.hearers:
In that world, marriages were usually arranged by families. A father or brother made the agreement, and gifts passed between the families. The groom's family gave gifts to the bride and her household. Laban, her brother, speaks first and takes a leading part.

That is a long way from how many people marry today, and it should not be made to look like a modern love story. Rebekah's family speaks for her. But notice what the text adds. They ask her. And she answers with one Hebrew word: ‘I will go’.

Readers differ on what she was asked. Some think it was only whether to leave now or after ten days. Others think it was her consent to the marriage itself. Either way, her voice is heard, and her answer is firm. She chooses to leave everything she knows, for a man she has never met, in a land she has never seen.

Her blessing echoes God's promise to Abraham after the binding of Isaac. God said Abraham's descendants would ‘possess the gates of their enemies’ (22:17). Rebekah's family, without knowing it, blesses her with the same words.

Rebekah's ‘I will go’ also echoes Abraham's own going. God told Abraham to go from his country and his father's house (12:1). Now Rebekah does the same.
passages.later:
God's word to Abraham was “Your descendants will possess the gates of their enemies” (Genesis 22:17), and here it is spoken over Rebekah.

The family line runs on: “Abraham was the father of Isaac, Isaac the father of Jacob” (Matthew 1:2). Rebekah becomes one of the mothers of Israel, and the line leads to Jesus.

Ruth makes the same kind of choice, leaving her own land for a family and a God not her own (Ruth 1:16).
passages.asks: Rebekah said ‘I will go’, as Abraham once went. Ask what God may be asking you to step into without seeing the whole road. Then ask whether you let the people in your care have a voice in what happens to them.

passages.happening:
Isaac has come from Beer-lahai-roi and is living in the Negev (verse 62). “Early in the evening, Isaac went out to the field to meditate, and looking up, he saw the camels approaching” (verse 63).

Rebekah looks up and sees Isaac, and gets down from her camel (verse 64). “Who is that man in the field coming to meet us?” “It is my master,” the servant answered. “So she took her veil and covered herself” (verse 65).

The servant tells Isaac everything (verse 66). “And Isaac brought her into the tent of his mother Sarah and took Rebekah as his wife. And Isaac loved her and was comforted after his mother’s death” (verse 67).
passages.hearers:
Beer-lahai-roi is the well where Hagar met ‘the God who sees me’ (16:13-14). Isaac lives near it. The family that used Hagar ends up drinking from the well she named.

Isaac is in the field ‘to meditate’. The Hebrew word is rare and its meaning is not certain. Many think it means to pray or think quietly; some think it means to walk.

Both of them ‘looked up’. Then Rebekah covers herself with a veil. A veil marked a bride coming to her husband.

The chapter ends with three short, tender lines. He brought her into his mother's tent. He took her as his wife. He loved her. It is only the second time the Bible uses the word ‘love’ (the first was Abraham's love for Isaac, 22:2), and the first time it says a man loved his wife. And Isaac, who lost his mother three years before (by the ages in 23:1 and 25:20), was comforted.
passages.later:
Paul uses marriage as a picture of Christ and his people: “Husbands, love your wives, just as Christ loved the church and gave Himself up for her” (Ephesians 5:25). Revelation ends with a wedding: “the marriage of the Lamb has come, and His bride has made herself ready” (Revelation 19:7).

Some older Christian writers read the unnamed servant as a picture of the Holy Spirit bringing a bride to the Son. That is an allegory, a reading that treats each person as a symbol; the text and the New Testament do not say it.
passages.asks: The chapter ends with grief and love in the same verse: Isaac loved Rebekah and was comforted after his mother's death. Ask whom God has given you to love, and whether you have let that love comfort you. Then notice that the last word of the chapter is comfort.
